title: Pilot Model
description: A pilot model is any model of a product built to evaluate a business component's design or resolve technological uncertainty under IRC Section 41.
summary: A pilot model is any representation or model of a product built to evaluate a business component's design or resolve technological uncertainty under IRC Section 41 and Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4(a)(3)(ii). For U.S. taxpayers claiming the federal R&D tax credit, materials and wages spent building and testing pilot models qualify as QREs when the work precedes commercial production.

body.text: A pilot model is any representation or model of a product built to evaluate a business component's design or resolve technological uncertainty under IRC Section 41 and Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4(a)(3)(ii). For U.S. taxpayers claiming the federal R&D tax credit, materials and wages spent building and testing pilot models qualify as QREs when the work precedes commercial production.
Executive Summary and Regulatory Baseline

Within the statutory and administrative architecture of the United States Research and Development (R&D) Tax Credit under Internal Revenue Code (IRC) Section 41 and Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4, the pilot model—commonly referred to in engineering and tax practice as a prototype—serves as the primary physical or digital manifestation of qualified research. While the statutory text of IRC Section 41(d) establishes the overarching definition of qualified research without explicitly defining the word "prototype" in the statutory provisions, Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4(a)(3)(ii) and Treasury Regulation § 1.174-2(a)(4) legally define a pilot model as any representation or model of a product that is constructed to evaluate a business component's design or to resolve technological uncertainty during the development or improvement of that component. Functionally, a pilot model encompasses preliminary models, computer-aided simulations, experimental test builds, or full-scale experimental articles fabricated during the development lifecycle to evaluate one or more technical alternatives concerning a business component, whether that component takes the form of a tangible product, manufacturing process, computer software system, technique, invention, or chemical formula.

The classification of an experimental unit as a pilot model carries substantial financial and tax compliance consequences for corporate taxpayers across manufacturing, life sciences, and technology sectors. Unlike standard commercial inventory produced for routine customer distribution, a pilot model is inherently experimental in character; its principal function at the time of construction is technical validation, structural evaluation, and hypothesis testing rather than commercial sale. When a taxpayer constructs a pilot model to test competing design hypotheses or overcome engineering constraints, the raw materials consumed in its construction and testing—alongside the direct, supervisory, and support labor incurred—are eligible for 100% inclusion as Qualified Research Expenses (QREs) under IRC Section 41(b)(2), supplemented by 65% of eligible third-party Contract Research Expenses (CREs) under IRC Section 41(b)(3)(A). Conversely, if an article is classified as routine commercial production or preproduction scaling, the underlying material expenditures must either be capitalized into inventory as Cost of Goods Sold (COGS) under IRC Section 471 and Section 263A or capitalized and depreciated over multiple tax periods under IRC Section 167 and Section 168, thereby forfeiting immediate R&D tax credit eligibility.

Because the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) applies heightened examination scrutiny to claims involving custom fabrication, first-of-kind commercial manufacturing, tooling, and trial production runs—and enforces rigorous business-component-level reporting requirements on Form 6765 (Credit for Increasing Research Activities)—taxpayers must establish a clear, contemporaneous documentary nexus between each pilot model iteration and the statutory Four-Part Test. Establishing this audit-ready trail requires tracing how engineering uncertainties regarding capability, method, or appropriate design necessitated the construction of sequential pilot models, documenting the systematic process of experimentation applied to those models, and segregating eligible experimental supply and wage expenditures from post-experimentation commercial production costs.
Statutory and Regulatory Framework: The Pilot Model Under the Four-Part Test
Definition of a Pilot Model and the Three Qualification Pillars

Under Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4(a)(3)(ii) and the parallel rules governing research and experimental expenditures under Treasury Regulation § 1.174-2(a)(4) (finalized in Treasury Decision 9680), a pilot model represents the tangible or digital medium through which Qualified Research Activities (QRAs) are conceived, tested, and validated. Treasury Regulations specify that a pilot model includes a fully functional representation or model of a product—or, to the extent that the "shrinking-back rule" of Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4(b)(2) applies, a discrete component or subassembly of that product—produced to evaluate and resolve uncertainty concerning the product during its development or improvement. For expenditures associated with a pilot model to qualify under IRC Section 41(d), the underlying activities must satisfy all four prongs of the statutory test, which administrative practice and judicial precedent distill into three operational pillars specific to pilot model evaluation.

First, the activity must address the resolution of technological uncertainty under IRC Section 41(d)(1)(A) and Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4(a)(3). This means the pilot model is initiated and constructed to answer an unresolved technical question where information available to the taxpayer does not establish whether a specific capability can be achieved, what engineering or manufacturing method must be employed, or what appropriate design configuration will satisfy functional specifications. Even if the taxpayer knows at the outset that it is technically feasible to construct a product, uncertainty exists if the taxpayer is uncertain of the appropriate design or architecture required to achieve the desired performance or reliability target.

Second, the fabrication and testing of the pilot model must occur within a structured process of experimentation under IRC Section 41(d)(1)(C) and Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4(a)(5). Under the statutory "substantially all" rule codified in Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4(a)(6), at least 80% of the research activities measured on a cost or another consistently applied reasonable basis must constitute elements of a process of experimentation. This process requires identifying the uncertainty, identifying one or more alternatives intended to eliminate that uncertainty, and conducting a systematic evaluation of those alternatives utilizing modeling, simulation, or systematic trial and error.

Third, the pilot model must satisfy an evaluative functional use criterion. Under Treasury Regulation § 1.174-2(a)(4) and § 1.41-4(a)(3)(ii), the ultimate disposition of a pilot model does not control whether the costs of constructing it qualify as research expenditures. Although an experimental unit may eventually be sold to a customer or utilized in the taxpayer's trade or business after experimentation concludes and uncertainty is resolved, its original purpose at the time of construction must be technical evaluation and uncertainty resolution rather than the fulfillment of a routine customer order lacking design risk. If a whole product does not independently satisfy the Four-Part Test because its overarching architecture is already established, the shrinking-back rule of Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4(b)(2) mandates applying the Four-Part Test at the level of the most significant subset of elements—such as an experimental subassembly, sensor module, or control algorithm pilot model—until either a qualifying subcomponent is isolated or the most basic element of the product fails the statutory criteria.

Activities under IRC § 41(d)(1)(B)(i) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(4) must fundamentally rely on principles of the hard sciences, specifically physical science, biological science, engineering, or computer science.
Demonstrates the direct application of scientific and engineering principles through metallurgical or polymer selection, structural geometry, fluid dynamics, or algorithmic architecture.
Elimination of Technological Uncertainty
Under IRC § 41(d)(1)(A) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(3), information available to the taxpayer at the outset does not establish the capability, method, or appropriate design of the business component.
Signals that standard engineering calculations and publicly available technical data were insufficient to guarantee performance without constructing and testing an experimental unit.
Process of Experimentation

Under IRC § 41(d)(1)(C) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(5)–(6), substantially all (80% or more) of the activities must constitute elements of a systematic process of evaluating alternatives via modeling, simulation, or systematic trial and error.
Embodies the iterative design-build-test-redesign cycle across sequential pilot model versions (e.g., V1.0 through V4.0) to compare technical alternatives against objective performance metrics.

body.text: The Evidentiary Value of Pilot Model Failure and Destructive Testing

A recurring vulnerability in R&D tax credit substantiation is the operational tendency of corporate engineering teams to preserve technical records only for the final, successful commercial design while discarding documentation, CAD files, and test logs associated with intermediate failures. From an IRS examination standpoint, however, the documented failure of an early pilot model provides the strongest possible contemporaneous evidence that genuine technological uncertainty existed at the outset of the project and that a bona fide process of experimentation was undertaken.

When engineering teams subject Pilot Model 1.0 or Pilot Model 2.0 to destructive stress testing, thermal cycling, fatigue loading, or algorithmic load testing to identify failure modes, structural limits, or material incompatibilities, the resulting failure analysis reports demonstrate conclusively that the appropriate design or manufacturing method was not readily ascertainable from standard engineering practice. Tracing how specific failure metrics in an initial pilot model necessitated formal engineering change orders (ECOs), material substitutions, structural geometry modifications, and the fabrication of subsequent experimental iterations establishes an auditable chain of systematic trial and error. This documented progression of hypothesis, physical or digital fabrication, test failure, root-cause diagnosis, and redesign directly satisfies the process-of-experimentation mandate of Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4(a)(5) and insulates the taxpayer's claim against IRS examiner challenges alleging routine engineering or commercial production.
Categorizing and Substantiating Pilot Model Qualified Research Expenses

Capturing the full financial value of pilot model development requires accurately segregating eligible experimental costs across the three primary statutory QRE categories defined in IRC Section 41(b): qualified supply expenses, qualified wages, and contract research expenses.
Qualified Supply Expenses: The Consumption Rule Versus Capitalization Risk

Under IRC Section 41(b)(2)(A)(ii) and Section 41(b)(2)(C), qualified supply expenses encompass amounts paid or incurred for tangible property directly used or consumed in the conduct of qualified research, provided that such property is neither land (or improvements to land) nor property of a character subject to the allowance for depreciation. Treasury Regulation § 1.41-2(b)(1) confirms that supplies used in the general and administrative conduct of the business do not qualify, whereas raw materials, electronic subcomponents, chemical compounds, custom polymer blends, sensors, and metal alloys directly consumed during the fabrication and destructive testing of pilot models are 100% includable as QREs when properly substantiated.

A primary compliance hazard emphasized in the IRS Audit Techniques Guide: Credit for Increasing Research Activities (i.e., Research Tax Credit) (Research Credit ATG) is the statutory boundary between consumable experimental supplies and depreciable capital assets. IRS examiners scrutinize pilot model expenditures to determine whether the constructed model itself, or any of its constituent subassemblies, possesses an enduring economic useful life in the taxpayer's business operations that renders it subject to an allowance for depreciation under IRC Section 167. If a pilot model is a temporary article destroyed during stress testing, scrapped upon completing experimental validation, or stripped of economic utility once design uncertainty is resolved, its material costs qualify in full as consumable QRE supplies.

Conversely, if a purported pilot model is a durable, functional capital asset subsequently retained by the taxpayer for multi-year commercial production, internal plant operations, or ongoing commercial display without depreciable-property exclusion, the asset itself may be characterized as property of a character subject to depreciation under IRC Section 41(b)(2)(C)(ii), disqualifying its underlying material acquisition costs from QRE supply treatment. Furthermore, while Treasury Regulation § 1.174-2(a)(4) clarifies that the eventual sale of a pilot model does not retroactively invalidate the experimental nature of the development activity under Section 174, taxpayers claiming supply QREs under IRC Section 41(b)(2)(C) must ensure that experimental supply costs are properly segregated from depreciable tooling and routine commercial inventory accounts.
Qualified Wages: Direct, Supervisory, and Support Labor Allocation

Employee wages typically represent the largest quantitative share of an R&D tax credit claim. Under IRC Section 41(b)(2)(A)(i) and Treasury Regulation § 1.41-2(c), qualified wages encompass Form W-2 compensation (as defined in IRC Section 3401(a)) paid or incurred for employees performing "qualified services" across three distinct operational tiers defined in IRC Section 41(b)(2)(B). The primary tier consists of engaging directly in qualified research, which covers time spent by mechanical, electrical, chemical, and software engineers, industrial designers, and research scientists directly defining technical design requirements and experimental specifications, constructing digital simulation models or physical pilot model iterations, executing performance tests and destructive stress protocols, and conducting post-test failure analysis and iterative redesign sessions. The second tier encompasses the direct supervision of qualified research, capturing time spent by first-line technical managers, laboratory directors, or principal engineers directly overseeing pilot model testing protocols, reviewing experimental test telemetry, and directing design modifications on the shop or laboratory floor, while excluding higher-tier executive or administrative oversight. The third tier covers the direct support of qualified research, including time spent by skilled machinists, CNC operators, laboratory technicians, or quality-assurance specialists preparing raw materials, assembling experimental pilot model fixtures, calibrating test rigs for an experimental run, or cleaning and resetting testing apparatus immediately following destructive pilot model trials.

Furthermore, under the "substantially all" wage rule of IRC Section 41(b)(2)(B) and Treasury Regulation § 1.41-2(d)(2), if at least 80% of an employee's total services during the taxable year consist of qualified services on pilot models and other qualified research activities, 100% of that employee's eligible Form W-2 wages for the taxable year may be included as QREs. Defending wage allocations during an IRS examination requires linking employee Form W-2 Box 1 wage records and payroll registers to granular, contemporaneous project time-tracking logs or substantiated engineering allocation studies that specify the exact business component and pilot model version, such as "Prototype V2.0 Testing".
Qualified Contract Research Expenses: The 65% Rule and Unfunded Research Mandate

When a taxpayer lacks internal fabrication equipment or specialized testing facilities and engages external third-party specialists to fabricate experimental subcomponents or perform specialized laboratory stress testing, metallurgical analysis, or environmental validation on a pilot model, those payments are evaluated as Contract Research Expenses (CREs). Under IRC Section 41(b)(3)(A) and Treasury Regulation § 1.41-2(e)(1), eligible CREs are generally limited to 65% of the gross amount paid or incurred by the taxpayer to any non-employee person for qualified research services performed on the taxpayer's behalf. This 35% statutory reduction reflects Congress's presumption that a third-party vendor's gross invoice includes overhead, administrative costs, and profit margins that would not qualify if the research were performed in-house.

To claim contract research expenditures for pilot model fabrication or testing, the underlying contractual arrangement between the taxpayer and the vendor must satisfy the "on behalf of" and "unfunded research" requirements of Treasury Regulation § 1.41-2(e)(2)–(3) and IRC Section 41(d)(4)(H). Specifically, the contract must be entered into prior to the performance of the qualified research, the agreement must state that research services are being performed on behalf of the taxpayer, the taxpayer claiming the credit must retain substantial rights in the resulting pilot model design and research findings, and the taxpayer must bear the financial risk of failure. Bearing financial risk requires that payment to the third-party vendor is contingent upon the performance of the research services rather than contingent upon the successful functional outcome of the pilot model. If a third-party vendor is paid only upon delivering a fully validated, guaranteed-performance unit ("pay-for-success" or fixed-price commercial acceptance contract where the vendor bears the cost of failed iterations), the expense is treated as an acquisition of a commercial product or funded research rather than a qualified contract research expenditure for the purchasing taxpayer.

body.text: Hypothetical Worked Example: Financial Impact of Capturing Pilot Model QREs

To illustrate the exact financial mechanics of pilot model cost classification, consider a worked example of a mid-sized engineering firm developing an experimental business component during a single tax year. Suppose the firm incurs fixed qualified engineering labor wages (Wq) of $100,000 directly attributable to designing, fabricating, and testing a pilot model. In addition, the firm expends $100,000 on specialized raw materials (high-strength steel alloys, precision sensors, chemical compounds, and embedded electronics) consumed across destructive pilot model iterations (Stotal), evaluated across progressive substantiation tiers from $0 to $100,000 in increments of $25,000 (or $5,000 granular steps in dynamic modeling). In an extended scenario, the firm also pays $50,000 in gross fees (Cgross) to an independent metallurgical laboratory for destructive stress testing under an unfunded prior-to-performance contract where the engineering firm bears full financial risk and retains all design rights. Applying the baseline model's estimated net R&D tax credit rate (rnet = 10% of total QREs, reflecting a standard regular credit after IRC Section 280C(c) reduction or simplified credit benchmark) and the statutory QRE inclusion percentages (100% for qualified wages and supplies; 65% for qualified contract research) yields distinct financial outcomes across progressive levels of pilot model substantiation.

In Scenario A (Misclassification of Pilot Model Supplies as COGS), the firm fails to substantiate the experimental units as pilot models under Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4(a)(3)(ii), requiring the entire $100,000 in material expenditures to be capitalized into inventory as standard Cost of Goods Sold ($0 eligible supply QREs, leaving $100,000 in uncaptured COGS). Consequently, total QREs consist solely of qualified engineering wages:

Estimated Net Tax Credit<sub>A</sub> = 0.10 × $100,000 = $10,000

In Scenario B (Substantiation of $25,000 in Pilot Model Supplies) and Scenario C (Substantiation of $50,000 in Pilot Model Supplies), the firm implements partial inventory and scrap controls that substantiate $25,000 and $50,000 of consumed pilot model materials, respectively, while the remaining unsubstantiated materials ($75,000 in Scenario B; $50,000 in Scenario C) remain capitalized as COGS. For Scenario B, total QREs reach $125,000 ($100,000 + $25,000), generating an estimated net tax credit of $12,500. For Scenario C, 100% of the $50,000 substantiated supply cost is added to QREs:

In Scenario D (Substantiation of $75,000 in Pilot Model Supplies) and Scenario E (Full Substantiation of $100,000 in Pilot Model Supplies), progressive refinement of engineering scrap and consumption logs captures $75,000 (yielding $175,000 in QREs and a $17,500 net tax credit, with $25,000 remaining in COGS) and ultimately all $100,000 of experimental pilot model materials. When all $100,000 of consumed materials are substantiated in Scenario E, uncaptured COGS drops to $0 and total QREs double relative to the labor-only baseline:

Estimated Net Tax Credit<sub>E</sub> = 0.10 × $200,000 = $20,000

The Exclusionary Boundary: Pilot Model Experimentation Versus Commercial Production

A foundational statutory limitation under IRC Section 41(d)(4)(A) is the explicit exclusion of any research activity conducted after the beginning of commercial production of the business component. Because the pilot model defines the operational frontier of experimentation, pinpointing the exact chronological and technical moment when the pilot model phase terminates and commercial production commences is critical to audit defensibility.
Defining the Commercial Readiness Threshold

Under Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4(c)(2)(i) and IRS administrative guidance, any activity conducted after the beginning of commercial production is excluded from qualified research. A business component is deemed ready for commercial production at the point when it has been developed to the point where it is ready for commercial sale or use, or meets the taxpayer's basic functional and economic requirements for the component's sale or use. Once a pilot model successfully validates the underlying design hypothesis, eliminates the capability, method, or design uncertainty, and satisfies these basic functional and economic criteria, the research phase concludes. All subsequent expenditures transition immediately from qualified experimentation to non-qualifying commercialization, preproduction planning, and manufacturing scale-up activities.
Non-Qualifying Post-Prototype Activities and the Debugging Distinction

Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4(c)(2)(ii) and IRS Audit Techniques Guides enumerate six specific categories of post-prototype activities deemed to occur after the beginning of commercial production that are categorically excluded from QRE treatment. Specifically, these per se excluded activities encompass preproduction planning for a finished business component, tooling-up for manufacturing and commercial assembly, conducting trial production runs, troubleshooting aimed at detecting faults in production equipment or manufacturing processes, accumulating data relating to commercial production processes, and debugging flaws in a business component after commercial production has begun. Because manufacturing taxpayers face heightened IRS audit scrutiny regarding custom fabrication, production tooling, and first-article manufacturing runs, differentiating between experimental pilot model iterations designed to resolve technical uncertainty and preproduction activities aimed at scaling a proven design is essential. Note, however, that if a taxpayer is developing a fundamentally new or improved manufacturing process as a separate business component under IRC Section 41(d)(2)(B)—distinct from the product being manufactured—experimental pilot line trials resolving uncertainty in the manufacturing process itself can qualify until that process meets its basic functional and economic requirements.

A frequent point of contention during IRS examinations is the operational distinction between debugging fundamental design flaws during the pilot model phase and debugging commercial production flaws after commercial readiness is achieved. Both Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4(c)(2)(ii)(F) and the IRS Audit Guidelines on the Application of the Process of Experimentation for All Software treat debugging flaws in a business component after commercial production begins as an excluded activity. If a pilot model has not yet met basic functional and economic requirements and undergoes iterative troubleshooting to resolve architectural, structural, or material capability uncertainties, that activity constitutes qualified R&D prior to commercial production. Conversely, once the final pilot model establishes the appropriate design and capability, subsequent efforts to resolve assembly-line yield issues, fix manufacturing equipment faults, or optimize an already functional process for mass-production throughput or unit-cost reduction must be excluded from QREs—even if those production-scaling efforts involve practical trial and error on the factory floor.
Navigating the Commercial Readiness Threshold for Digital Pilot Models

While physical manufacturing offers observable transition markers—such as issuing purchase orders for hard production tooling, freezing the bill of materials (BOM), or reconfiguring commercial assembly lines—determining when a digital pilot model (such as software architecture, machine-learning algorithms, distributed data structures, or finite-element CAD simulations) crosses into commercial readiness is significantly more complex. As modern engineering workflows increasingly rely on rapid digital prototyping and virtualized simulation prior to or in lieu of physical fabrication, taxpayers must establish objective internal controls to demarcate the end of qualified research.

Substantiating the commercial readiness boundary for digital pilot models requires maintaining formal version-control repositories (such as Git commit histories), alpha/beta sandbox environment logs, architectural decision records (ADRs), formal release-readiness sign-off reports, and pre-established quantitative performance, latency, and reliability benchmarks. Documenting the precise software build or code commit at which the digital pilot model resolved all core algorithmic and architectural uncertainties allows the taxpayer to capture 100% of eligible developer wages (and eligible cloud computing rental costs used directly in hosting experimental development sandboxes under IRC Section 41(b)(2)(A)(iii) and Treasury Regulation § 1.41-2(b)(4)) during the experimental phase while cleanly excluding post-release code maintenance, user-interface polishing, and routine bug patches.
Industry-Specific Pilot Model Scenarios and Case Analyses

The operational application of pilot model rules under IRC Section 41 and Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4 varies across technical disciplines depending on the nature of the business component, the physical versus digital medium of experimentation, and the governing regulatory environment. Three primary industry scenarios illustrate how the statutory boundary operates in practice: advanced medical devices, custom manufacturing equipment, and financial technology software.
Advanced Medical Devices: Multi-Iteration Sensor Array and Clinical Validation

In highly regulated sectors such as medical device engineering, pilot model experimentation encompasses both iterative physical fabrication and mandatory pre-commercial regulatory validation. Consider a medical technology company developing a portable diagnostic medical device centered on a proprietary sensor array business component designed to operate under extreme, variable biological conditions. At the outset of development, the engineering team confronts two primary technological uncertainties under Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4(a)(3): first, determining the appropriate material composition (design uncertainty) necessary to ensure biological compatibility while preserving structural integrity across severe internal pressure and temperature cycles (capability uncertainty); and second, devising a specialized manufacturing integration process (method uncertainty) to mount the delicate sensor array inside the compact device housing while maintaining required electromagnetic and electrical shielding without degrading mechanical reliability.

To resolve these uncertainties through a systematic process of experimentation under Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4(a)(5), mechanical and electrical engineers first construct digital pilot models using computer-aided design (CAD) and multiphysics simulation software to narrow candidate geometries and thermal/mechanical material properties, generating qualified wage expenses. Subsequently, because simulation alone cannot establish biological and mechanical performance under real-world tolerances, the team fabricates sequential physical pilot models (Versions V1.0 through V4.0), systematically varying custom polymer blends and metal alloys alongside modified injection-molding parameters and bespoke Computer Numerical Control (CNC) machining programs. Each physical version undergoes rigorous laboratory performance, resilience, and destructive safety testing, where test failures in V1.0 through V3.0 drive iterative redesigns culminating in V4.0.

Across this multi-stage development cycle, raw materials consumed and scrapped across failed versions V1.0 through V3.0 and validation units of V4.0 qualify at 100% as supply QREs under IRC Section 41(b)(2)(C); engineering and technician hours spent on hands-on fabrication, stress testing, and failure analysis qualify at 100% as wage QREs under IRC Section 41(b)(2)(B); and external laboratory fees paid under unfunded contracts for environmental and biocompatibility validation qualify at 65% as contract research QREs under IRC Section 41(b)(3)(A). Crucially, because clearance or approval from the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) acts as a mandatory legal and functional prerequisite before a diagnostic medical device can be commercially marketed or sold, subsequent pre-commercial clinical trials and validation testing required to confirm safety, efficacy, and the appropriate design and capability of the business component prior to regulatory clearance remain squarely within the qualified experimentation phase prior to the beginning of commercial production.
Custom Manufacturing Equipment and Software Development Scenarios

Beyond medical devices, the distinction between a qualified pilot model and routine commercial activity applies directly to industrial equipment fabrication and enterprise software development. In custom manufacturing, consider a company designing an automated mechanical jig to hold complex structural parts for a high-speed robotic welding system. Although the company understands basic mechanical clamping principles, genuine uncertainty exists regarding whether the proposed fixture geometry can maintain micron-level structural stability under dynamic robotic welding thermal and mechanical loads. The engineering team constructs Pilot Model Version 1 (V1) to test the design hypothesis; during experimental welding trials, V1 vibrates excessively and ruins the weld seam. Engineers perform root-cause vibration analysis and fabricate a redesigned Pilot Model Version 2 (V2) incorporating modified structural dampening geometry. Under Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4(a)(3)(ii), the structural metal, vibration sensors, and direct engineering and machinist labor used to build and test both the failed V1 unit and the redesigned V2 unit qualify in full as QREs because the units served as pilot models resolving capability and design uncertainty prior to commercial readiness.

Similarly, in financial technology (Fintech) software development, consider a company developing a novel machine-learning fraud-detection algorithm designed to identify complex, real-time synthetic identity anomalies without increasing transaction latency. Because existing heuristic models cannot achieve the target false-positive reduction within sub-millisecond execution windows, software engineers construct and deploy a non-commercial "Sandbox" beta build—functioning as a digital pilot model—to test competing neural-network architectures and feature-weighting algorithms against historical transaction datasets. Even though the pilot model exists entirely in software code rather than physical metal or polymers, 100% of the developer wages incurred while coding, configuring, and testing the sandbox build qualify as QREs prior to commercial deployment, whereas routine post-release code maintenance and customer support activities after production deployment are excluded.

body.text: Documentation, Substantiation, and IRS Audit Defense Strategy
Form 6765 Project-Level Disclosure Requirements

Recent tightening of IRS administrative compliance—most notably the expanded Section G business-component disclosure requirements on revised Form 6765 (Credit for Increasing Research Activities) and the heightened refund-claim specificity rules under Chief Counsel Advice (CCA) 20214101F—has made granular, project-level substantiation mandatory for audit survival. Vague, high-level cost aggregations or generalized cost-center estimates risk summary procedural rejection or full disallowance upon examination under the recordkeeping mandate of IRC Section 6001 and Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4(d).

For every pilot model claimed on Form 6765, contemporaneous documentation must directly satisfy the three foundational scoping inquiries utilized by IRS examiners and engineers to audit R&D claims. First, the taxpayer must establish unambiguous identification of the business component ("what was created") by explicitly naming each specific business component and its corresponding pilot model iterations—such as "Prototype V3.0 of the Diagnostic Sensor Array" or "Pilot Model V2 of the Robotic Welder Fixture Jig"—and classifying the component type across product, process, computer software, technique, formula, or invention categories. Second, the documentation must establish the qualification nexus ("why the activity qualifies") through a specific technical narrative explaining the initial capability, method, or design uncertainty existing at the start of the project and tracing the systematic process of experimentation—including CAD modeling, simulation, sequential physical prototyping, and destructive testing—employed to evaluate alternatives and resolve that uncertainty. Third, the taxpayer must provide granular cost accounting ("how much the activity cost") by maintaining a project-by-project financial bridge that breaks down QREs across qualified employee wages (categorized by direct conduct, direct supervision, and direct support), consumed pilot model supplies, and eligible third-party contract research expenditures tied to that specific business component.

body.text: Institutional Roadmap for Pilot Model Compliance

To eliminate audit adjustments and maximize the capture of eligible pilot model expenditures, organizations conducting engineering, manufacturing, and software R&D must institutionalize five interconnected operational controls across their engineering and accounting departments.

At the governance level, companies should establish a formal "Qualified Research Gate Review" process that integrates R&D tax specialists directly into engineering stage-gate reviews prior to releasing any pilot model for commercial scaling. Formally recording the exact milestone, date, and engineering sign-off at which a pilot model satisfies its basic functional and economic requirements under Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4(c)(2)(i) creates an objective, audit-defensible cutoff. This bright-line boundary ensures that the organization captures 100% of legitimate experimental design, fabrication, and testing costs prior to the gate while systematically excluding post-gate preproduction planning, commercial tooling, and trial production runs.

In parallel with stage-gate governance, financial controllers should segregate General Ledger (GL) accounts and implement granular inventory tracking within enterprise resource planning (ERP) and procurement systems. Creating dedicated General Ledger codes for "R&D Prototype Materials" wholly separate from standard "Raw Materials," "Work in Process (WIP)," or "COGS" accounts—and tagging material requisitions allocated to "experimental pilot model runs" (QRE) versus "pilot production runs" (non-QRE)—ensures strict adherence to the IRC Section 41(b)(2)(C) supply consumption rule and prevents the accidental capitalization of consumable experimental supplies into commercial inventory.

To reinforce these accounting controls with indisputable physical evidence, engineering teams should conduct periodic "Scrap and Fail" audits to identify physical models that were discarded, reworked, or destroyed during testing. Pairing written failure analysis reports and destructive test logs with a timestamped photographic and video archive of sequential pilot model iterations (e.g., V1.0, V2.0, and V3.0) visually proves the systematic process of experimentation to IRS examiners and refutes any contention that the units were routine commercial goods or depreciable capital equipment.

Finally, organizations must align their ongoing engineering workflows directly with Form 6765 project narratives and benchmark internal practices against published IRS Audit Techniques Guides (ATGs). Training engineering leads to record design iteration summaries, performance test reports, and material specifications using the statutory framework of IRC Section 41 ensures that contemporaneous technical records translate seamlessly into compliant Form 6765 business-component disclosures. Proactively reviewing the general Research Credit ATG, the Audit Guidelines on the Application of the Process of Experimentation for All Software, and sector-specific IRS directives (such as the Aerospace and Pharmaceutical ATGs) enables corporate tax departments to anticipate examiner scrutiny regarding depreciable property boundaries, shrinking-back documentation, and software commercial-readiness thresholds well in advance of filing.
Statutory and Regulatory Verification Matrix

cells: The U.S. R&D Tax Credit is governed by Internal Revenue Code (IRC) Section 41, which defines qualified research in IRC § 41(d) without explicitly defining the word "prototype" in the statutory text.

IRC § 41(d) sets forth the Four-Part Test for qualified research; the explicit legal definition of "pilot model" (and prototype) is established by Treasury Regulations rather than the statutory text itself.

Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4(a)(3)(ii) (alongside Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(a)(4)) legally defines a pilot model (prototype) as any representation or model of a product constructed to evaluate a component's design or to resolve technological uncertainty.

Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(3)(ii) defines a pilot model as any representation or model of a product (or subcomponent under the § 1.41-4(b)(2) shrinking-back rule) produced to evaluate and resolve uncertainty concerning the product during its development or improvement.

The Four-Part Test requires satisfying Permitted Purpose (business component functionality, quality, reliability, or performance), Technological in Nature (hard sciences: engineering, physics, biological or computer science), Elimination of Technological Uncertainty (capability, method, or appropriate design), and Process of Experimentation (≥ 80% substantially all threshold evaluating alternatives via modeling, simulation, or trial and error).

Qualified Supply Expenses (raw materials consumed in fabricating and testing pilot models) are 100% includable in QREs under IRC § 41(b)(2)(C) provided they are tangible property neither capitalized as commercial inventory (COGS) nor of a character subject to an allowance for depreciation.
Confirmed under IRC § 41(b)(2)(C), which defines supplies as tangible property other than land/improvements and property of a character subject to depreciation.

The IRS Research Credit Audit Techniques Guide (ATG) instructs examiners to scrutinize prototype/pilot model expenditures to determine whether the model or subcomponents are durable assets subject to an allowance for depreciation versus consumed or scrapped experimental models.
IRS Audit Techniques Guide: Credit for Increasing Research Activities (i.e., Research Tax Credit), Chapter 3 (Substantiation and Recordkeeping / Supplies).

IRS examiners specifically audit large supply claims and custom fabrication prototypes to verify that capital assets placed in service in the taxpayer's operations are not claimed as consumable supplies.

Qualified Wages under IRC § 41(b)(2)(B) are 100% includable for employees directly engaged in pilot model design, fabrication, testing, failure analysis, and redesign, as well as first-line direct supervision and direct support personnel, substantiated via Form W-2s, payroll registers, and project-level time tracking.
Also incorporates the 80% "substantially all" rule of IRC § 41(b)(2)(B) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(d)(2) for employee wage inclusion.

Contract Research Expenses (CREs) paid to third parties for specialized pilot model fabrication or laboratory testing are generally limited to 65% of eligible expense under IRC § 41(b)(3)(A) and must be unfunded under IRC § 41(d)(4)(H) (taxpayer retains substantial rights and bears financial risk of failure).

Research conducted after the beginning of commercial production (when the business component is ready for intended sale/use or meets basic functional and economic requirements) is excluded under IRC § 41(d)(4)(A); per se excluded activities under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(c)(2)(ii) include preproduction planning, tooling up, trial production runs, troubleshooting production equipment/processes, accumulating production data, and post-commercial debugging.
IRC § 41(d)(4)(A); 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4(c)(2)(i)–(ii); IRS Software Process of Experimentation Audit Guidelines.
